newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai stocks plunge on greater risk vs region - Daiwa.
newsitem.headline: Thai stocks plunge on greater risk vs region - Daiwa.

text.p: Thailand's equity market has plunged because of the greater risk of investment in Thailand compared to other Asian markets, a regional strategist for Daiwa Institute of Research said on Tuesday.

"Thailand carries a greater degree of risk than other markets in the region because it does have a high current account deficit and it does have a high foreign debt level by Asian standards," Peter Perkins told a seminar.

The Thai bourse closed on Tuesday again at a more than three-year-low of 956.34. On Monday foreign investors fled as the index fell 6.0 percent, offloading mainly bank stocks and underweighting their positions in Thai stocks.

Thailand's current account deficit stood at 8.1 percent of gross domestic produc (GDP) in 1995. Although the Bank of Thailand forecast that the gap would be narrowed to 7.8 percent of GDP this year, some economists said the deficit may be higher.
Perkins predicted there would be no instant Thai turnaround even when a new government assumed office following the November 17 election.
"It will be December by the earliest, and more likely February, before we are able to determine if the Thai economy is to face another six months of difficulty," he said.
Perkins said commercial banks' loan portfolio quality remained a serious concern.

"It appears to have put investors, especially international investors, off tremendously. What worries me is that I think the Bank of Thailand lacks the flexibility to address loan portfolio quality problems in a very short period of time."
Perkins added investors were being discouraged by the possibility of renewed pressure on the baht, which last came under speculative attack in late July and early August.

"I think the risk is relatively limited. But if things keep heading in their current direction then I think investors will be more cautious about investing here because of concerns about the vulnerability of the baht."
But he said downside in the equity market was now limited, and Daiwa had maintained a neutral long term stance on the market.

"Expectations have deteriotrated to such an extent I believe the rate of further deterioratation is declining. For the most part I think the market will stabilise as soon as news stops getting worse and it's hard to see news getting too much worse than today," Perkins said.
